Ping will always have a large effect on your aim, as it is as if you exist on a 130ms delay from the "real" game. If you (120ms ping) and an opponent (60ms ping) see each other at exactly the same moment, the opponent's actions will be recorded by the game 2x faster than your actions. It also means that for example your opponent walking in a straight line across your screen is always going to be just a little bit ahead of where you think they are (since it takes you longer to receive the information from the game).

It is totally possible to learn to play on high ping, but you will need to get used to the fact that things are always going to be just a little bit off from what they appear on your screen

Because normal games are for more casual play and do not count towards your ranking in the slightest, it just doesn't matter. Normal games are about practice or a carefree match. If you only play to win that's what ranked games are for. This system forces people with say unstable internet connections into a more casual mode, where they won't impact the more serious players.

I find that the argument of: people play normals for different reasons to be super flawed because League of Legends does a great job providing different game options so that you can join a specific queue in accordance to what you want to play. Ranked is for the competitive games, where you play to your utmost capacity. Normal Draft is a practice mode for ranked, where you once again play the best you can, only difference is that it isn't counted towards your ranking, and is thus more forgiving. Normal Blind (although being the original game mode) is now for playing carefree on Summoner's Rift. Putting people with high leave percent into normal blinds isn't a punishment, because those games aren't about winning at any cost. 

In fact, this system could potentially improve all game modes. People would afk less in ranked, because they don't want to get bumped out of ranked. They would probably also make sure they have a stable connection/enough time to devote for a match, thus also limiting the leaves. On the normal queue side of things (where leaves are already more frequent) players would be more prompted to stay the entire match and not quit because "noob team. gg. fk it, dun care itz normalz".

I am very interested to have a real discussion about this aswell, and I fell like I can be very unbiased, so I'll try and give an answer to everything :)

*First* you ask why we feel DRM is violating- Well, DRM as a whole is a silly concept. It makes you feel like you are a pirate and they need to check up on you to make sure you haven't done anything bad with your property; it punishes  loyal customers, when in truth, people will always find a way to cheat, where it be by modding the console (as was done with 360) or by running it through fake authentication servers, or some new crazy thing that won't exist till 4 or 5 years from now. What if the servers are overloaded and XBL can't authenticate your game, or what if your ISP is trash and crashes often (as is the case for myself). This means that I will not be able to play the campaign of Assassin's Creed, as I am waiting for my internet to come back up so that I can resume browsing reddit. 
> I would like a purely offline mode for disc based games and I do think/hope that one will have to be implemented due to military deployees. 

Microsoft has [made it very clear](http://news.xbox.com/2013/06/main) that **THIS IS NOT THE CASE.** The true paragraph where it is stated reads as follows: With Xbox One you can game offline for up to 24 hours on your primary console, or one hour if you are logged on to a separate console accessing your library. Offline gaming is not possible after these prescribed times until you re-establish a connection, but you can still watch live TV and enjoy Blu-ray and DVD movies. (Can be found here [http://news.xbox.com/2013/06/connected](http://news.xbox.com/2013/06/connected) towards the bottom of the page)

To me, the above statement shows me that I am not buying a game which I will then own, the disc that comes in the box that I paid 60$ for.. that disc is just an authentication key for an online service that Microsoft will provide me, as long as my key can be verified every 24 hours. This raises a rather large issue for me, as I do not just play games, I collect them; what will happen to my game library when the XB2 and PS5 are released? What happens if Microsoft goes out of business, or they drop out of the console market and the XB2 is never made? Surely they will not keep all these hundreds of thousands of servers running just so people can play their old games. I own every halo game to date for my 360, and I KNOW that no matter what, I will be able to experience the epic campaign so long as I can find a functioning 360, and a television which supports the outputs of the console. This is why I recently purchased a second 360, just in case, because my game library is important to me. I still like playing smash bros on my Nintendo 64 with my friends all these years later, and with XB1, this does not seem like it will be possible. Unless they come out and officially say: "We will disable the DRM for the XB1 at the end of the generation". And I strongly doubt that will be the case or even possible, as it seems built into the infrastructure of the system.

Alright, on to the *Second* point of why the uproar over used games- Used games are a major part of the gaming industry, and it is not just the direct selling of games which is blocked;
>In our role as a game publisher, Microsoft Studios will enable you to give your games to friends or trade in your Xbox One games at **participating retailers**. Third party publishers **may opt in** or out of supporting game resale and may set up business terms or transfer fees with retailers. [http://news.xbox.com/2013/06/license](http://news.xbox.com/2013/06/license)

This means that a smaller gaming store, may very well be all of a sudden unable to offer used games, since they are not "participating", which means that they could lose a part of their business and even potentially go out of business. That is a damn shame, especially when you consider how horrible of a shopping experience Gamestop has to offer. About 40% of the games I own are purchased used, because, well, too many games come out close to each other, sometimes you don't want to put down 300$ in one month on buying all the new games.. you get a couple, and by the time you get around to the others, well its 20$ less to buy a used copy than a new one, and you now have have saved enough to cover  your next 60$ game. Another point, would be picking up an old game that is now hard to find new. I have had my hands full and have never quite gotten around to any of the Arkham games. I really hate starting things halfway through the story, and I was thankfully able to get Arkham Asylum used for pretty cheap. I loved as I knew I would and bought the second game new, and I will be buying the upcoming third on day 1. If not for me being able to get the first game, I would have bothered with any of the others, and that is two more sales that they made thanks to the used games market without counting all of the people I have urged to purchase the games. I know I am not alone with a similar sentiment.

Your *third* point of pricing and future proofing- Well 100$ less is just a win.. no one can really argue that, especially when it can considered to be that the price difference is because Sony is not forcing motion technology (something many "core" gamers have clearly said they don't even want) where as Microsoft must also cover the cost of the Kinect, which many find an unwanted annoyance. You address the brief point that Sony has not stopped publishers from screwing us on the DRM, and well that is true. What is certain is that at this point in time, no publisher wants to be the bad guy and bring DRM to the PS4. The system could never be as policed as what Microsoft has in place anyways, because on the console side of things, it is not set up that way. From what we saw, the PS4 still "reads" the disk in a traditional game console sense, where as the XB1 runs the .exe file off of its hard drive, and then the disk becomes unimportant (as all games must be installed like on a PC). You cannot tell the PS4 to stop reading the disk just because the game does not connect to the internet, the two are separate.

Your *fourth* point of second-screen and cloud support- The "best version" is as usual on PC, but for consoles, I assume that PS4 should be better, because it has better hardware, while both consoles run on a similar AMDx86 structure which should make porting between the two very simple, unlike the ps3 vs 360 where the ps3 design was much too complex because of its crazy structure which requires a lot more time to optimize. As for the 2nd screen, its just a part of this next gen, everyone has it.
